title: Information Technology Act, 2000 — Section 3 (Digital Signature Authentication)

content.overview: Section 3 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides that subject to the provisions of the section any subscriber may authenticate an electronic record by affixing his digital signature. Authentication is effected by the use of asymmetric crypto system and hash function which envelop and transform the initial electronic record into another electronic record such that certain integrity and attribution properties hold, as the section enacts.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Is authentication by digital signature claimed? (2) Asymmetric crypto system and hash function used as required? (3) Subscriber relationship? (4) Link to s. 3A electronic signature?
content.study:
s. 3 is about digital signature authentication technique. s. 3A introduced electronic signature more broadly. Do not conflate the two.

No new case invented.

sections.heading: Authentication power
sections.body: Any subscriber may authenticate an electronic record by affixing his digital signature, subject to the section.

sections.heading: Technique
sections.body: Authentication by asymmetric crypto system and hash function transforming the initial electronic record as the section provides.

sections.heading: Integrity properties
sections.body: The technique is designed so that any alteration of the record or signature is detectable and the signature is uniquely linked to the subscriber — as enacted.

sections.heading: Link to s. 3A
sections.body: s. 3A recognises electronic signature more broadly, including digital signature as one form; both must be read together.

sections.heading: Method
sections.body: Identify claimed authentication method; check statutory technique; relate to secure electronic record rules where relevant.

examples.title: Contract signed digitally
examples.body: Parties authenticate an electronic contract by digital signatures under s. 3 technique — authentication analysis follows the statutory crypto/hash requirements.

hypotheticals.question: Is a typed name at the end of an email a digital signature under s. 3?
hypotheticals.analysis: s. 3 contemplates authentication by asymmetric crypto system and hash function; a mere typed name does not satisfy that technique.

distinctions.title: s. 3 digital signature vs s. 3A electronic signature
distinctions.left: Authentication specifically by digital signature (asymmetric crypto/hash).
distinctions.right: Broader electronic signature concept, of which digital signature is one form.

misconceptions.trap: Any electronic mark is a digital signature under s. 3.
misconceptions.correction: s. 3 requires the specified authentication technique using asymmetric crypto system and hash function.
